MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: Despite a wave of Iranian attacks since the beginning of October, total Middle Eastern crude oil flows (ex-Iran) remain resilient. Flows are becoming, however, lumpier (days of multiple tanker crossings followed by days of very few tankers). 

Overall, Middle East (ex-Iran) crude flows, including Strait of Hormuz plus all the bypass routes, are holding at ~75% of pre-war levels, down from a ~95% *peak* in the last days of September. Crucially, despite the drop in recent days, the Oct 1-Oct 10 period average remains above Sep full month average (and well above full month August). Kuwait is struggling the most right now. UAE, Iraq and KSA (the last one using both Persian Gulf and Red Sea) are doing relatively well.

All said, the risk is to the downside if the Iranian attacks continue (and if they become more successful). Iran has sunk at least one container ship in the SoH over the last 24 hours. The same goes for Red Sea flows under Houthi / Iraq militias potential attacks. For Iran itself, Hormuz remains closed.

One key indicator to follow: despite the Iranian attacks against SoH traffic, the physical premium for Middle Eastern crude has come down significantly in recent days, touching today a near 2½-month low.

How AI for the enterprise is evolving, from owning a task to owning an outcome:

1. Assistant: handles one task in seconds, like sending a follow-up email. Companies pay for it out of their software budget.

2. Agent: handles one interaction in minutes, like a customer's refund call. It takes on work people used to do, so it gets paid for out of the labor budget.

3. Long-running agent: works toward a goal for weeks or months, like getting an injured client the biggest settlement possible. Because it owns the result, the company selling it can price on the outcome it delivers.

Nathan Lambert, former post-training co-lead at the Allen Institute for AI, now launching Trillium, a nonprofit open AI lab, joins a16z's Lisha Li to discuss whether open models can really keep up with the frontier.

When he tells researchers in China that an average OpenAI researcher reportedly has five thousand H100s to work with, "their jaw just falls to the floor." In his view, Chinese labs have the talent but are mostly short on compute.

He also thinks the distillation story is overblown. Based on the research, he puts its edge at a few months, and says "there's a bit of cope" in thinking only American labs can build good models.

A lot of frontier progress outside math and code comes down to labs buying 1) data and 2) RL environments. It's a multibillion-dollar market, and some of it is sloppy enough to teach models to reward hack.

That's a big part of why Trillium exists. Nathan wants to give away the environments other people would sell, and show exactly how his team uses AI to build AI, including where the models still get stuck. His bet is that the more people can see how this works, the better prepared everyone is for what's coming.

Until recently, AI agents mostly handled short tasks, like one support call or one email. Now they can stay on a job for weeks or months.

That matters for "relay race" work that runs through a long chain of people.

Every handoff in that chain is a chance for something to fall through: a slow callback, a dropped follow-up, lost context.

Take a personal injury case. Today it moves from intake to investigation to the demand letter, with different people at each step. A single case agent can work it from the first call to settlement, chasing witnesses, records, and bills, and keeping the client and attorney updated along the way.

The same idea applies to processes like mortgages, insurance claims, and enterprise sales.

Because the agent owns the end result, the company selling it can charge on the outcome (a closed loan, a settled case, a signed deal) and move past pricing on the labor it saves (paralegal hours, call center seats).

Full piece from a16z's @dhaber on long-running agents in high-value customer journeys: https://t.co/aHaatcizcd

80% of us will trust an AI answer even if it's false (⁠╥⁠﹏⁠╥⁠)

Found a great independent study on how people follow advice from LLMs, and the results are very frustrating.

Here’s what they did:

1,372 participants answered seven Cognitive Reflection Test trick questions (9,593 total trials), either alone or with an embedded ChatGPT assistant.

The researchers controlled the assistant to give either the correct answer or a confident wrong one.

They tracked AI use, whether people followed it, accuracy, and confidence. Later studies added time pressure, then incentives plus immediate feedback.

Results:

Participants used AI on over 50% of trials and usually copied it, following correct AI ~93% of the time and wrong AI ~80%.

AI also boosted confidence even when wrong.

Ouch.

Frontier AI labs like Anthropic are being valued on the same scarcity premium once given to L1s.

Investors watched that premium fade once blockspace became abundant. Usage kept growing even as each transaction earned less. 

Open models, distillation and model routing are now expanding the supply of intelligence in the same way.

According to Bloomberg, Anthropic’s revenue reportedly grew from $4.6B in 2025 to an annualized run rate above $65B by July 2026. But its rumored $2T IPO valuation is at odds with its growing compute expense and poor public narrative campaign.

Pricing pressure would hit harder because most of Anthropic’s compute spending is locked in. Roughly 80% of the $518B it has reportedly committed to cloud and compute cannot be canceled. 

Revenue carries no such guarantee, since many of its largest clients reportedly have no long-term contract.

thread_tweets.text:
Some choice quotes from the report: 

Banks as cops: these efforts distracted the banks from objective assessments of financial risks and increased the risk of misuse by some to refuse service to subjectively disfavored customers or industries. Moreover, it put banks in a quasi-legislative position of limiting banking services—or imposing values-based conditions on the availability of banking services—for lawful businesses disfavored by some activists and political leaders who lack the legal basis or legislative power to restrict or outlaw these business activities

Mere allegations: Mere allegations, negative press, or negative reviews contributed to some banks declining to serve average Americans, even in the absence of any validation of the underlying facts or concerns; yet some banks were able to find ways to get comfortable with the reputation risks posed by high-net-worth clients.

Inconsistency: The OCC found that, in response to general reputation risk policies, bank employees escalated customers or prospective customers that held potentially contested viewpoints outside the perceived “mainstream” and that those views were often equated with higher potential reputation risk. The OCC found that decisions related to such escalations were not universally consistent across transactions the OCC sampled, illustrating the subjective nature of the banks’ ambiguous and open-ended reputation risk policies

NGOs: The banks also relied on various sources to inform these decisions, including the results of negative news searches and non-traditional sources, such as the opinions of advocacy organizations

Whipsaw: When banks rely on difficult-to-quantify factors to decide whether to provide financial services, there is significant risk that bank decisions will whipsaw back and forth with the current political or social climate. This report confirms that value judgments and assumptions regarding the current views held by elected officials and policy makers can factor into banks’ decision making. The report also observes that as the political and social climate changed, so too did banks’ application of industry restrictions. Past experience suggests that industries may continue to suffer this whipsaw effect with the change of each administration or Congress, even in the absence of statutory changes.

But only if you’re willing to admit when you’re wrong.

When you look at how $QQQ or S&P is constructed, you realize how hard it is to outperform it over the long term. It has an incredible balancing effect. 

Yes, every now and then you find a great opportunity with very little risk, but those opportunities usually come only once or twice a year. The rest of the time, holding indices and maybe 2–3 stocks is a very smart strategy. 

I think you’re being very honest with yourself, and that’s important. I’ve often gone back to holding indices when I realized my stock picks weren’t working. Instead of praying they’ll recover or telling everyone how great they are, I stop and reflect on what I’m doing wrong. That’s radical honesty, and I think it’s one of the most important qualities in trading.

i wanted a physical version of my ai agent. Something real in the living room that shows my to-do list and my day, and that my wife can see too.

I bought a seeed reterminal e1002, an e-ink display. e-ink because it looks like paper: no glow, no buzz, it just sits there like a note on the wall (almost)

setup was honestly simple:
- built the open-source muse gadget firmware on my computer with my sdk token in it
- flashed it to the device over usb
- paired it in the muse app (settings, devices, developer mode) thanks @natfriedman 

now every morning at 7am my agent renders my briefing (calendar, top to-dos, weather) and pushes it to the screen. my wife reads it over coffee. it basically became the family's shared to-do list

whole thing took ~20 min. your agent doesn't have to live in a chat window. give it a physical representation!
